title: The AI Habits Rubric: Grade How Students Use AI, Not Just What They Turn In
author: How to Teach With AI
source: How to Teach With AI, July 13, 2026
summary: With AI pervasive in student work, the author argues that grading only outputs is now the wrong pedagogical layer—like grading only answers in a math class while ignoring method. The post proposes a three-criterion AI Habits Rubric designed to make invisible student processes visible and give teachers shared language for feedback, integrity conversations, and meaningful recommendation letters. The three criteria are: Intentional Use (did the student use AI purposefully at specific stages, or just dump the prompt and submit whatever came back); Metacognitive Reflection (can the student evaluate AI output, catch errors, and identify what they still need to learn); and Intellectual Honesty (is the student transparent about what they produced versus what the AI produced). Each criterion maps to concrete artifacts—AI use statements, annotated chat logs, reflection blocks, and draft-before-AI evidence—that make the process auditable rather than guesswork. The author advises framing the rubric as coaching, not surveillance: position yourself as developing a real skill, not catching cheaters, and introduce requirements incrementally. The rubric's deepest value is generating semester-long evidence of how a student thinks—evidence specific enough to transform recommendation letters from generic praise into genuine testimony.
points: Grading only outputs in an AI world is like grading only the math answer while ignoring the method—the learning lives in the process, and that process must now be made visible through concrete artifacts.

The three rubric criteria map to three auditable questions: Did the student have a plan before opening AI? Can they evaluate AI output and catch its errors? Are they transparent about the line between their work and the AI's?

Concrete artifacts—AI use statements, annotated chat logs, reflection blocks, draft-before-AI evidence—transform assessment from vibes-based guessing into a teaching surface that can actually be improved.

The critical framing shift is from 'did you cheat?' (which makes students hide) to 'show me your process' (which makes students talk)—positioning the teacher as a coach developing a real skill, not a cop catching cheaters.

A semester-long record of AI habits gives teachers evidence for recommendation letters with genuine specificity: not 'strong critical thinker' but 'consistently evaluated AI output, identified errors, and reflected on what they still needed to learn.'
quotes: You also know you have no systematic way to tell the difference between a student who used ChatGPT to sharpen their thinking and a student who pasted the assignment prompt into ChatGPT and submitted whatever came back.
Grading only outputs in an AI world is like grading only the answer in a math class and wondering why nobody learns the method.
If a student can use AI effectively but can’t reflect on that use, they are one tool update away from being lost.
A student scoring high on this criterion can walk you through their AI use the way a carpenter walks you through their toolbox.
When the question is “did you cheat,” students hide. When the question is “show me your process,” students talk.
Your students are already developing AI habits. The question is whether those habits are visible enough for you to actually teach them something.
